4.1.summary:
A healthy mind doesn't need things to go to plan. When your judgement is working as it should, it adjusts to whatever is actually possible, keeps its aim, and turns obstacles into material for its own work.

Marcus compares it to fire. A small flame is smothered by what's thrown on it, but a strong fire seizes the same heap, burns it and blazes higher because of it. Setbacks only put you out if your inner fire is weak.
4.1.today: The train is cancelled, so the journey becomes time to read. The project gets cut back, so you learn to do more with less. A difficult relative at a family gathering becomes a chance to practise patience instead of a ruined afternoon.

4.2.summary: Don't do things aimlessly. Every action should have a point, and it should be done properly, following sound principles the way a good craftsperson follows the rules of their trade. Marcus treats living well as a skill you practise, not something that happens by drifting.
4.2.today: Before picking up your phone, opening another tab or agreeing to another meeting, ask what it's actually for. If there's no answer, that's usually the sign to leave it.

4.3.summary:
You don't need a holiday cottage or a beach to get away from it all. You can retreat into your own mind at any moment, provided you've stocked it with a few short, solid principles to come back to. Calm, for Marcus, is simply a well-ordered mind.

He then runs through the usual complaints, such as other people's behaviour, your lot in life, bodily pain and the itch for fame, and answers each, ending every time with "be quiet at last". Two thoughts matter most: things outside can't touch your mind, since the upset comes from your opinion of them, and everything you see is already changing and passing away.
4.3.today: When the inbox, the news and the family group chat all pile up at once, you can't always book a weekend away. But you can take five minutes on a bench or in the car park, go over a couple of things you know to be true, and come back steadier.

4.4.summary:
Marcus builds a chain of reasoning: all humans share the capacity to reason; reason tells us what to do and not do; so we share a common law; so we're fellow citizens of one community, and the whole world is a kind of city.

He adds that our minds must come from somewhere, just as our bodies are made of earth, water and fire drawn from the world around us. Nothing comes from nothing, so our reason too belongs to something larger that we all share.

4.5.summary: Death is as natural as birth. Birth brings certain elements together; death takes them apart into the same elements again. There's nothing shameful or unnatural about it, and nothing that goes against what a reasoning being is. Marcus wants you to see death as a normal process of nature, not an outrage.

4.6.summary:
People act according to their character, and it's as pointless to expect otherwise as to expect a fig tree not to produce sap. When someone behaves badly, that's what someone like them does.

Then Marcus adds a sobering thought: before long both you and they will be dead, and soon after even your names will be forgotten. The grievance is very small set against that.
4.6.today: The relative who always makes a dig at dinner, the neighbour who always parks badly: they'll keep doing it, because that's who they are. Being outraged every time is like being shocked that the kettle gets hot.

4.7.summary: Harm starts with your opinion. If you drop the judgement that you've been harmed, the feeling of being harmed goes, and with it the harm itself. Marcus isn't denying that things happen to you, but that most of the injury lies in how you interpret them.
4.7.today: A colleague doesn't reply to your message. Tell yourself you've been snubbed and you'll stew all afternoon. Drop that story and it's just an unanswered message, probably because they're busy.

4.8.summary: Real harm is anything that makes you a worse person. If something doesn't do that, it doesn't make your life worse either, whatever it costs you in comfort, money or status. For Marcus, the only damage that counts is damage to your character, and nothing outside can do that to you.

4.9.summary: This is a brief, cryptic note. Marcus seems to be telling himself that whatever has just happened was necessary, because the way the universe works serves the good of the whole and had to bring it about. What looks like misfortune to you is part of what keeps everything running.

4.10.summary:
Everything that happens is fair, if you look closely enough. Marcus doesn't just mean that events follow from one another in sequence, but that each thing gets what it is due, as if handed out by someone who judges rightly.

He tells himself to keep looking at the world this way, and in everything he does to hold on to one aim: being a genuinely good person, in the full sense of the word.

4.11.summary: When someone wrongs you, don't take on their view of things, or the view they'd like you to have. If they think insulting you makes you smaller, or want you to feel humiliated, you don't have to agree. Look at what actually happened, as it really is.
4.11.today: When someone online calls your opinion stupid, they want you to feel stupid. You can check whether the criticism has any substance and leave the rest, instead of accepting their verdict along with their tone.

4.12.summary:
Keep two rules ready. First, act only as your reason directs, for the good of other people. Second, be willing to change your mind when someone shows you you're wrong.

But the change has to come from being genuinely convinced that the new view is fairer or better for everyone, not because it's more comfortable or will make you look good.
4.12.today: In a meeting, someone points out a flaw in your plan. It's tempting to dig in to save face, or to fold just to be liked. The right reason to change course is that they're actually right.

4.13.summary: A quick exchange with himself. Do you have reason? Yes. Then why not use it? If your reason is doing its job, Marcus says, you have everything you need. The problem is rarely a lack of good sense, only a failure to apply it.

4.14.summary: You are a part of the universe, not separate from it. When you die you'll disappear back into the whole that produced you, or rather be absorbed and transformed into the creative force that keeps making new things. Marcus finds this a calm, even fitting, thought about death.

4.15.summary: Picture many grains of incense on one altar. One drops into the fire first, another a little later, and it makes no difference which. Marcus is thinking of human lives and deaths: whether yours ends sooner or later hardly matters in the end, since all go the same way.

4.16.summary: People who now think of you as an animal could see you as almost godlike within ten days, if you go back to your principles and to living by reason. Marcus means that respect isn't won by status or cleverness but by how you live, and it can come back fast once you return to what matters.

4.17.summary: Don't live as if you have ten thousand years. Death is always hanging over you. So while you're alive and still can, be good. Marcus isn't being morbid. He's reminding himself not to put off becoming the person he means to be.
4.17.today: Think of the apology you keep postponing, the friend you've meant to ring for months, or the habit you'll fix "after this busy spell". There may not be an after.

4.18.summary: You save yourself a great deal of trouble when you stop watching what other people say, do or think, and focus on whether your own actions are fair and decent. Marcus quotes a saying he attributes to Agathon: don't look around at other people's bad behaviour, but run straight to the finish without swerving.
4.18.today: Scrolling through what others are posting, keeping score of who in the office gets away with what, or reading the comments to see who's wrong: all of it pulls you off your own lane. Your own work is enough to look after.

4.19.summary:
Wanting to be remembered after death makes little sense. Everyone who remembers you will die soon, then the people who remember them, until the memory goes out entirely. Even if your fame lasted for ever, what good would it do you, dead or alive?

Praise only matters if it's useful for something. Chasing it means neglecting what nature has actually given you to do now. The passage breaks off mid-thought.
4.19.today: It's the urge to build a legacy, have your name on a building or be the one people talk about at the leaving do. Marcus would ask who'll be around in a hundred years to care.

4.20.summary:
Beautiful things are beautiful in themselves. Praise doesn't add to them and criticism doesn't take away. That's true of a flower or a fine piece of work, and even more true of things like law, truth and kindness.

An emerald isn't worse for nobody admiring it. Marcus means the same applies to you: being good doesn't need applause to be good.
4.20.today: A well-made meal is just as good if no one photographs it, and a kind thing you do is no less kind if nobody hears about it. The likes on a post don't change what's in it.

4.21.summary:
Marcus tackles an old puzzle: if souls survive death, how is there room for them all in the air? His answer is that, like buried bodies breaking down to make room for new ones, souls last a while and are then transformed and taken back into the universe's creative fire. Countless animals are eaten every day, and the world absorbs them too by changing them into other things.

The way to think clearly about it, he says, is to separate a thing's material from what gives it its form.

4.22.summary: Don't get spun around by every impulse. Whatever you do, keep fairness in view, and whenever a thought or impression arrives, hold on to your judgement instead of being carried off by it. Marcus is describing a mind that stays steady while things move around it.
4.22.today: A sharp email arrives and you feel an instant urge to fire one back. That's the impression. Keeping hold of your judgement is pausing long enough to ask whether it actually deserves the reply you're drafting.

4.23.summary:
This reads almost like a prayer. Whatever suits the universe suits Marcus, and whatever comes in nature's good time is neither too early nor too late. Everything comes from nature and returns to it.

He borrows a poet's line in praise of Athens, "dear city of Cecrops", after its legendary first king, and asks why he shouldn't say "dear city of Zeus" about the whole universe.

4.24.summary:
An old philosophical saying advises doing few things if you want peace of mind. Marcus improves it: do what's necessary, and what reason tells a social creature like you to do. That brings the calm of doing things well as well as doing fewer of them.

Most of what we say and do is unnecessary, so keep asking whether this is one of those things. Cut unnecessary thoughts too, and the unnecessary actions won't follow.
4.24.today: Before saying yes to another committee, replying to every message in a thread or rewriting a slide for the fifth time, ask whether it's needed. The same goes for rehearsing an argument in your head on the way home.

4.25.summary: Try out the life of a good person and see how it suits you: someone content with their share of what the world hands out, and satisfied with acting fairly and being kind. Marcus frames it as an experiment, as though goodness is something you test by living it.
4.25.today: For one week, take what comes at work without complaint, do your bit honestly and be kind to whoever's in front of you. Then notice whether you feel worse, or a good deal lighter.

4.26.summary:
A string of quick reminders. Don't get worked up; keep things simple. If someone does wrong, they mainly harm themselves. Whatever happens to you was woven into the universe's pattern from the start. Life is short, so make the most of the present with good sense and fairness.

The last line is a warning: even when you relax, stay sober and in control of yourself.
4.26.today: When a friend lets you down, the damage is mostly to their own character, not yours. And the evening off is a chance to rest, not to drink or binge until you've lost the next morning.

4.27.summary: Whether the universe is ordered or a random heap, it's still a universe. And it makes little sense to find order in yourself but suppose disorder in everything else, when all things, however far apart, are connected and affect one another.

4.28.summary: A bare list of the worst kinds of character: dark, soft, stubborn, brutish, childish, stupid, false, coarse, deceitful, tyrannical. Marcus doesn't explain it. It reads like a note to himself of the traits he wants to watch for and avoid, perhaps with the tyrant at the end as the particular danger for an emperor.

4.29.summary:
Turning away from what happens in the world cuts you off from it. Marcus piles up images: the person who won't understand events is a stranger in the universe, a runaway from shared reason, blind, and poor because they depend on others for what they should find in themselves.

Worst of all is resenting what happens. The same nature that produced the event produced you, so rejecting it makes you like a boil on the body of the world, a piece torn off the community of reasoning people.
4.29.today: It's the person who refuses to read any news, or shuts out a family situation because they hate how it's going. Withdrawing in protest feels like strength, but it leaves you more isolated and less use to anyone.

4.30.summary: One philosopher has no tunic, another no books, another is half-naked and has no bread, yet each holds fast to reason without earning a living from it. Marcus seems to admire them: wisdom doesn't depend on possessions, and poverty needn't shake your principles.

4.31.summary: Love the skill you've learned, however modest, and be content with it. Live the rest of your life trusting everything to the gods wholeheartedly, and being neither anyone's tyrant nor anyone's slave. Contentment with your own work goes hand in hand with that freedom.
4.31.today: The plumber who takes pride in a neat job, the teaching assistant who loves the small moments in class: their work isn't glamorous, but it's theirs. Contentment there beats envying someone else's title or bossing people about to feel bigger.

4.32.summary:
Look back at the age of Vespasian, emperor about a century before Marcus. You'll see people marrying, raising children, falling ill, dying, fighting, feasting, trading, flattering, plotting and longing for high office. That whole world is gone. The same with the age of Trajan, and with every era and nation.

Think most about people you've known who chased trivial things and neglected what mattered. Give each thing the attention it deserves and no more, and you won't be dissatisfied.
4.32.today: Old photos of a busy high street in the 1950s show people rushing to work, worrying and shopping, and almost all of them are gone. Today's commuters and office feuds will look just the same one day.

4.33.summary:
Old words go out of fashion, and so do famous names. Marcus lists heroes of early Rome and the Republic, such as Camillus, Scipio and Cato, then the emperors Augustus, Hadrian and Antoninus, his own adoptive father. All have become stories, then forgotten. The ordinary dead vanish even faster, and even eternal fame is nothing.

What deserves serious effort is this: fair thoughts, actions that help others, honest words, and gladly accepting whatever happens as natural and expected.

4.34.summary: Hand yourself over willingly to Clotho, the Fate who in Greek myth spins the thread of each person's life, and let her weave it into whatever she likes. Marcus means accept your life as it unfolds, instead of fighting what has already been decided by forces bigger than you.

4.35.summary: Everything lasts only a day: both the person who remembers and the person who's remembered. Marcus puts fame in its place with a single line. Memory is as short-lived as what it holds on to, so living for others' recollection of you is building on sand.

4.36.summary: Everything comes about through change, and nature loves nothing more than changing what exists into new things like it. Everything that exists is in a sense the seed of what comes next. Marcus says it's a crude idea to think of seeds only as things planted in soil or a womb. Your own death, too, is part of the world making something new.

4.37.summary: You'll be dead soon, Marcus tells himself, and you still aren't simple, still get rattled, still suspect that outside things can hurt you, still aren't kind to everyone, and still don't see that wisdom lies only in acting justly. It's an honest self-reproach. He's measuring himself against his own ideals and finding the gap, with time running out.

4.38.summary: Study what drives people, even the wise: what they steer clear of and what they go after. Marcus suggests you learn most about someone's mind, their "ruling principle", from their choices about what to pursue and avoid, and that this is worth studying carefully.
4.38.today: Watch how a respected manager handles a mistake, or what a calm friend refuses to get drawn into. What they won't chase or argue about tells you more than any advice they give.

4.39.summary:
What feels bad to you isn't in someone else's mind, or in what happens to your body. It's in the part of you that forms opinions about what's bad. Stop forming that opinion and all is well.

Even when the body is cut, burnt or rotting, let your judgement stay quiet. Marcus's test: anything that can happen equally to good and bad people, like illness or pain, can't itself be good or bad.
4.39.today: A cold in the week of a big event, a badly broken arm, a long recovery. These happen to kind people and unkind people alike. They're hard, but they don't decide whether you're living well.

4.40.summary: Think of the universe as a single living creature, with one body and one soul. Everything is part of its awareness, everything moves together, and everything helps cause everything else. Marcus pictures it as thread being continuously spun and woven into a single cloth, with each life and event a strand in the same fabric.

4.41.summary: Epictetus, the former slave turned Stoic teacher whose ideas shaped Marcus, liked to say that you are a little soul carrying around a corpse. It's a deliberately stark image. Your body is already mortal matter, and what really makes you you is the mind that carries it.

4.42.summary: Change is neither bad nor good. It's no evil for things to be broken down, and no great good for things to be made. Marcus is evening out our feelings: we mourn endings and celebrate beginnings, but they're the same process seen from different ends.

4.43.summary: Time is a fast river of events. As soon as something comes into view it's swept past, and the next thing follows it. Marcus wants you to stop expecting anything to stay put, so its passing comes as no shock.

4.44.summary: Everything that happens is as ordinary and predictable as roses in spring or fruit in summer. That includes illness, death, slander and betrayal, and whatever else delights or annoys foolish people. Seeing these things as normal and seasonal takes the shock out of them.
4.44.today: Office gossip, a friend who lets you down, the winter flu: they're as regular as the seasons. Expecting them doesn't make them pleasant, but it stops you feeling singled out.

4.45.summary: Events aren't just one random thing after another, like items on a list. Each fits with what came before in a meaningful way. Just as everything that exists is arranged in harmony, what comes into being shows a remarkable connectedness. Marcus sees the world as a rational, joined-up whole.

4.46.summary:
Heraclitus, the early Greek philosopher who taught that everything is in flux, said each element dies into the next: earth into water, water into air, air into fire, and back.

Marcus adds more of Heraclitus's points. People forget where the road leads, quarrel with the very reason that runs the universe, and find everyday things strange. Don't go through life as if asleep, and don't simply repeat what you were taught, like a child copying its parents.
4.46.today: It's easy to sleepwalk through a day of habits, or to hold views just because your family always did. Every so often it's worth asking whether you actually believe something or just picked it up.

4.47.summary: If a god told you you'd die tomorrow or the day after, you wouldn't much care which, unless you were very small-minded. The difference is tiny. Marcus says the same is true of dying many years from now instead of tomorrow. Set against all of time, the gap is just as slight.

4.48.summary:
Think how many doctors who frowned over the sick have died, how many astrologers who predicted others' deaths, philosophers who lectured on immortality, conquerors and tyrants. Whole cities are gone, Helice swallowed by the sea, Pompeii and Herculaneum buried by Vesuvius.

Human things are brief and slight. So pass through your short time in tune with nature, and end it contentedly, like a ripe olive falling, grateful to the tree that grew it.
4.48.today: The surgeon, the expert on the news and the confident forecaster all face the same end as everyone else. Knowing that can make you gentler about your own short time, and more grateful for it.

4.49.summary:
Be like a rocky headland: the waves keep breaking on it, and it stands still and calms the water around it.

When something bad happens, don't think "I'm unlucky this happened", but "I'm lucky I can bear it without being crushed or afraid". It could have happened to anyone, but not everyone would bear it well. Does it stop you being fair, generous, self-controlled and honest? If not, it hasn't harmed what makes you human. Bearing it well is the good fortune.
4.49.today: Redundancy, a cancelled wedding venue, a diagnosis. The event isn't chosen, but how you carry it is. Someone who meets bad news with steadiness and kindness has something worth more than the luck they lost.

4.50.summary:
A simple, if well-worn, way to stop fearing death is to think of people who clung to life for a long time. What did they gain over those who died young? Long-lived men of Marcus's day, who buried many others, ended in the grave all the same.

The span between birth and death is short, full of trouble, poor company and a frail body. Against the endless time before and after, three days and three generations come to much the same.

4.51.summary: Take the short road, which is the natural one: say and do everything in line with sound reason. That spares you trouble, conflict, scheming and showing off. Doing the plainly right thing is simpler than all the manoeuvring to look good.
4.51.today: Instead of drafting a carefully angled email to make yourself look blameless, just say what happened and what you'll do. It's quicker, and there's nothing to keep track of later.
